clue.text: Interview expert about article in Die Welt probing multinational organisation

indicators.note: the word for an expert goes around the rest, as 'about' means surrounding here

parts.note: an ace is an expert

indicators.note: the German article pokes into the middle of the organisation's letters, as a probe goes in

parts.note: UN is the United Nations
die is a German definite article, as printed in the newspaper title Die Welt

explanation.surface: A specialist is grilled about a piece in a German newspaper investigating some multinational body.
explanation.walkthrough: Die Welt is a German newspaper, so its article is a German word, not an English one; 'probing' and 'about' are the two container signals.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience is a formal meeting or interview granted by someone important, such as an audience with the Pope.

clue.text: I'm half of 10 plus half of 16: what am I?

indicators.note: only the front half of each of the two cross-referenced entries is kept

parts.note: the solution to 10 across
the solution to 16 across

explanation.surface: A puzzle posing as a classic conundrum, asking the solver to identify the speaker from fractions of other answers.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of RIDDANCE (10 across) is RIDD and the first half of LEAD (16 across) is LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a puzzling question, and many traditional ones end with the challenge 'what am I?'.

clue.text: Something exploited by extractive industries?

indicators.note: the answer is mined out of the following words, as ore is extracted

explanation.surface: A general question about what mining and quarrying firms make use of.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is dug out from across the join of the last two words, and the whole clue also describes it: miners work a seam of ore.
explanation.definitionFit: Miners follow a seam of metal or mineral deposit through the rock, which is exactly what extraction targets.

clue.text: Recess leads to pupils enjoying awesome spring break

indicators.note: the picked letters are broken up and rearranged into a new order
the leading letters of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: A school recess sends students off to enjoy a great spring holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials P, E, A and S are rearranged. 'Recess' and 'break' both look like school holidays, but 'break' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular recess at the end of a church, usually behind the altar.

clue.text: Thorough scrutiny of dictator's publicity material

indicators.note: a dictator is here someone dictating, so the phrase is what that speaker says out loud

parts.note: a proper job is a thorough one; a gander is British slang for a look or inspection

explanation.surface: A look at the promotional output of an authoritarian ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant, which fits the answer's subject, but it means someone speaking words for others to write down. 'Have a gander' is British slang for 'take a look'.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is material spread to promote a cause or regime, a form of political publicity.

clue.text: Not allowed except when half-dropping pants

indicators.note: the word loses its back half, three of its six letters being dropped

parts.note: unless means except when
pants is British slang for rubbish, so awful

explanation.surface: Something is forbidden unless your trousers are half pulled down.
explanation.walkthrough: UNLESS loses half its letters to give UNL. In Britain, calling something 'pants' means it is rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unlawful is against the law, so it is forbidden or not permitted.

clue.text: Underground worker at empty platform in Barking

indicators.note: barking is slang for mad, so these letters go crazy and are rearranged
the word is emptied, leaving just its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A tube worker stands on a deserted platform at Barking station in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a London Underground station, but here it means mad. Shuffle AT, PM (the outer letters of platform) and IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitman works down a mine pit, so he is a miner working below ground.

clue.text: Marshal, on horseback, going west like a wild animal

indicators.note: in an across answer, west is leftwards, so the riding piece travels towards the front

parts.note: to line up troops is to marshal them, so line
a jockey on horseback is said to be up

explanation.surface: A lawman riding away westward resembles some untamed beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marshal' seems a cowboy-film sheriff, but it is the verb. LINE plus UP gives LINEUP; moving UP leftwards gives L-UP-INE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lupine means wolfish, describing the qualities of a wolf, which is a wild animal.

clue.text: Soldier on holiday regularly experienced irrational fear

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper

indicators.note: every other letter of the phrase is taken, at regular intervals

explanation.surface: A soldier on leave suffered from unreasoning terror.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters of 'on holiday' give N, O, I, A.
explanation.definitionFit: Paranoia is an unfounded suspicion or dread that others mean harm.

clue.text: Candid shot about to receive clearance

indicators.note: the short word for about takes in the rest, holding it within

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: shot means ruined or broken, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An unposed photograph is about to get approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Candid shot' looks like a photograph, but 'shot' (ruined) is the anagram signal, and 'to receive' has the short word for about hold the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting rid of something is clearing it away, as in good riddance to rubbish.

clue.text: What's the matter as lamp melts?

indicators.note: as solid wax melts, the letters lose shape and are re-formed

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is wrong when a lamp starts melting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's the matter' looks like an ordinary question, but it means 'what kind of matter it is'. A lava lamp's glowing contents suit the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Plasma is the fourth state of matter, an ionised gas, alongside solid, liquid and gas.

clue.text: Taking place before start of day disrupts aardvark's normal activity?

indicators.note: the letter breaks into the activity, interrupting it

parts.note: aardvarks feed on ants and termites, so their usual activity is ant-eating

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: The beginning of the day interrupts an aardvark's usual routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Aardvarks are also called antbears; the question mark covers the playful description of feeding on ants, and 'disrupts' signals the letter breaking in.
explanation.definitionFit: To antedate something is to precede it in time, so happening earlier than it.

clue.text: Young person's allowance preserved by rise

definitions.note: the 's is short for is, so the definition reads as a young person

indicators.note: the allowance is kept safe within the rise, as food preserved in a jar

parts.note: an ascent is a rise or climb
the dole is a British state allowance paid to the unemployed

explanation.surface: A teenager's pocket money is protected by an increase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allowance' suggests pocket money, but it is the dole, British unemployment benefit, which goes inside ASCENT.
explanation.definitionFit: An adolescent is a teenager, someone between childhood and adulthood.

clue.text: Clipped manner of speaking ultimately felt stupid

indicators.note: a clipped word loses its tail, the final letter being cut

parts.note: an idiom is a manner of speaking

indicators.note: the very last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone's terse way of talking finally came across as dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clipped' looks like a description of curt speech, but it cuts M off IDIOM. 'Stupid' is the noun, as in 'Hey, stupid!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid can be a noun naming a foolish person, as in 'Listen, stupid', which equals a fool.

clue.text: Discover auditor's penalised

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so this is the word as heard

parts.note: being fined is being penalised with a money charge

explanation.surface: An accountant reviewing the books discovers they've been punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant, but it means a hearer.
explanation.definitionFit: To find something is to come upon it or uncover it, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Live electrical cable?

definitions.meaning: to live a certain life, as in to conduct a quiet life
a flex connecting an appliance to the mains

explanation.surface: A cable carrying current, perhaps dangerous to touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' reads as an adjective describing the cable, but it is the verb, as in leading a quiet life.
explanation.definitionFit: One leads a life, so the verb fits 'live'; and a flex or wire connecting equipment is called by this name.

clue.text: Recognise complaint raising appropriation of tune by on-line charity

indicators.note: in a down answer, raising the letters means reading them upwards
the charity appropriates the tune, taking it into itself

parts.note: e, as in e-mail, stands for electronic or online
aid is charitable help, as in Live Aid
a song is a tune

explanation.surface: Someone spots a grievance after an internet charity takes over a melody.
explanation.walkthrough: E and AID hold SONG to give ESONGAID, which reads upwards. 'Complaint' looks like a grumble, but here it is an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor identifying an illness from its symptoms diagnoses it; complaint means ailment.

clue.text: Bulb's working, subject to receiving current

definitions.note: the 's is short for is, so the definition reads as a bulb

indicators.note: the two short words take the current symbol in between them

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
on can mean dependent on or subject to, as in on approval
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A light bulb is functioning, subject to taking in electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulb' and 'current' suggest a lamp, but the bulb is a vegetable. I is the physics symbol for current.
explanation.definitionFit: An onion is a vegetable that grows as a bulb under the soil.

clue.text: Place where one goes to be heard

indicators.note: the phrase is meant to be heard, so the word sounds like the toilet word

parts.note: a polite euphemism for the toilet, the loo in British English

explanation.surface: A lavatory doubles as somewhere to speak up and be listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: Loo is British slang for a toilet, the place one 'goes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieu means place, as in the phrase in lieu of, meaning in place of.

clue.text: Passing round drinks at home for example

indicators.note: the abbreviation goes around the other letters, encircling them

parts.note: a cat laps milk, so laps means drinks
in means at home

explanation.surface: A round of drinks being handed out at someone's house, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round drinks' suggests buying a round in a pub, but 'round' puts EG around LAPSIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Time elapsing is time going by, as with passing years.

clue.text: Innocent bishop to become a priest

indicators.note: one letter turns into another, the bishop becoming the a

parts.note: a lamb is an innocent person
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A guiltless churchman is elevated to the priesthood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Innocent' looks like a name of popes, but means a lamb; its B changes to A.
explanation.definitionFit: A lama is a Buddhist monk or spiritual teacher in Tibet.

clue.text: Host slicing Iberian chorizo

indicators.note: the answer slices through the words, lying across their join

explanation.surface: A host is cutting Spanish sausage for guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' suggests someone entertaining guests, but it is a TV presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: A news anchor presents a broadcast, the same role as a TV host.

clue.text: Run artist's work affiliated with university

parts.note: in cricket, an extra is a run not scored off the bat
a mural is a painting on a wall

explanation.surface: A painter's picture is displayed on a campus.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bat-and-ball game, an extra is a run conceded via wides, no-balls and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Extramural courses are run by a university for people who are not full-time students.

clue.text: Take out 16 guns after shelling Cork?

indicators.note: the word has its outer shell removed, so only the inside letters remain

parts.note: a cork is a plug for a bottle

explanation.surface: Guns are dismantled after a bombardment of the Irish city of Cork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cork' looks like the Irish city and 'shelling' like gunfire. The 16 is LEAD (16 across), an electric cable.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling an electrical flex from its socket disconnects it, which is what unplugging means.

clue.text: Nico repeated shows having symbolic quality

indicators.note: what the doubled name shows is its inside, once the outer letters are shed
the name is written twice in a row

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Reruns of programmes featuring Nico have a symbolic feel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' signals the answer lying inside NICONICO, the name written twice, between its first N and last O.
explanation.definitionFit: Something iconic serves as an emblem or symbol, like a revered image.

clue.text: Most costly stones cut by revolutionary blade

indicators.note: the blade cuts into the stones, sitting between them

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for the weight a stone, here written twice for two stones

indicators.note: a revolutionary turns things round, so the word is reversed

parts.note: an epee is a fencing sword

explanation.surface: The priciest gems are sliced by a radical's knife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stones' looks like gems, but a stone is a British unit of weight (14 lb), shortened to st, used here twice; 'revolutionary' turns the blade round and 'cut by' puts it between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep prices are high ones, so the superlative means the most expensive.

clue.text: Author leaving upset farewell drink

indicators.note: the author departs, so that letter is removed
in a down answer, upset turns the word upside down so it reads upwards

parts.note: adios is Spanish for goodbye
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A writer departs after an emotional goodbye drink.
explanation.walkthrough: ADIOS reads upwards as SOIDA and loses I, the setter speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is a fizzy soft drink, or soda water used as a mixer.

clue.text: Former City boss?

parts.note: ex means former
EC is the postcode for the City of London

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone was once a boss in the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcodes begin EC.
explanation.definitionFit: An executive is a senior manager, informally shortened to this word.

clue.text: Embittered lives one school nurtures

indicators.note: the school holds the other letters within it, as nurturing protects

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
is means exists, so lives

explanation.surface: A bitter person's life is shaped by the school that raised them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' looks like a place of learning, but it is a group of whales, a pod.
explanation.definitionFit: Feelings that are poisoned have been spoilt by resentment, making someone bitter.

clue.text: Horse covered in spangles almost from nose to tail

indicators.note: from front to back the word is cut short, losing both its first and last letters

parts.note: something sequined is covered in sparkly spangles

explanation.surface: A horse decked out with sparkles from head to tail, nearly.
explanation.walkthrough: SEQUINED loses its end letters S and D. 'Horse' is the adjective-like use, as in horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: Equine means relating to horses, and 'horse' used before a noun works in the same way.
